content:
Earlier this year, I swapped my gas-powered mower for a robotic mower controlled by an iPhone. You need to manually drive the machine along the perimeter of your yard once, and the system will create a virtual map. Once set up, it will automatically mow according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tried another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think it might be more convenient and easier to use for many people.

Automatic camera mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I previously reviewed lies in how each system understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses RTK base station positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the perimeter with my phone to create the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. It has three built-in cameras, allowing the mower to automatically map the lawn area without burying boundary wires underground or installing a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process clearly takes longer. But I think this method may be simpler for people who are less familiar with technology.

To test this idea, I had my mom, who lives in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, without any assistance from me throughout the entire process. She replied that everything worked fine. Honestly, I was rather doubtful she would have the patience to manually drive the robot along the perimeter and manually mark no-go zones.

The automatic mapping produced a small odd issue in my front yard. Since there is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, the TerraMow initially included part of my neighbour's lawn within the coverage area of my map.

I resolved the issue by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, if there is no clear visible boundary line between two lawns, extra caution is needed during the initial mapping stage.

Seeing the world through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also support one of my all-time favourite features. The iPhone app can display a real-time view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to stream this footage in a larger window. I could sit comfortably indoors and watch the mower cross the backyard from its own perspective.

This feature is not essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun and occasionally helps explain why it slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 does not have a similar camera streaming feature.

The two iPhone apps are fairly similar in other respects. Both allow you to schedule jobs, adjust mowing modes, set zones, mark no-go areas, and remotely control the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly excellent design feature for this last function. In addition to the traditional left and right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone in a normal posture and steer the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone is not the primary use of either system. Ideally, the robot should operate on a schedule without any human intervention. However, the TerraMow's joystick is very practical for cleaning up missed spots.

Sometimes, it almost feels like using telepathy to control the robot (and it's quite satisfying). I can hold the iPhone down at my side, and with just slight thumb movements, the machine will head in the direction I want.

Every robotic mower app should emulate this control method.

More aggressive mowing performance

For me, the TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and also produced more noise while operating.

I wouldn't say the TerraMow is loud, but the difference between the two is very noticeable. The Anthbot can operate extremely quietly—so quiet that even if it's mowing with its headlights on after dark, it's easy to forget it's still running.

Since TerraMow relies on camera navigation, it requires daylight to operate reliably, making it more important to schedule it to mow during the day.

The V1000 feels solid and sturdy out of the box, and is also larger in size than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage with the product to cover the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage must be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow operates reliably and stably. I relied on it continuously for several weeks, completely without having to do any routine mowing myself.

When smart mapping becomes too clever

The same visual intelligence that makes the TerraMow easy to set up occasionally backfires.

The mower constantly adjusts the map based on what it sees. Saving these changes after each mow takes some time, during which you cannot perform other operations in the app.

After several consecutive days of heavy rain, I encountered an interesting edge case. Part of the yard had standing water, and the TerraMow intelligently avoided that area during its next operation.

Within the skipped circular area, the grass grew taller. As time passed, the mower seemed to treat these taller patches of grass as something to continuously avoid, and even after the standing water had long dried up, that patch of grass was never mowed again.

I used the app's remote control function to manually drive the mower through the taller grass, and the problem was resolved. Once that area returned to the appearance of a normal lawn, automatic mowing resumed as usual.

Regularly trimming the edges also helps the TerraMow handle boundary areas more decisively. If tall grass grows at blurred boundaries, it may be mistakenly identified as an obstacle and excluded from the mowing area.

The Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive and relies more on user-defined boundaries and obstacles. This method requires more upfront work, but it also avoids the situation where the map "changes its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac Review

After trying both systems, I lean toward recommending the TerraMow's camera approach for most people.

For me, underground boundary wires were not an option from the start, and installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining an additional piece of hardware. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation is not perfect. Initial mapping takes longer, hard-to-identify boundaries require manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook tall grass for a permanent obstacle.

These issues are all manageable. In exchange, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable and stable automatic mowing, fun real-time camera footage, and the best robotic mower app manual control experience I have seen.

I actually enjoy yard work, but mowing is the most repetitive part of it. After handing this task over to a robot, I can devote more time to landscape design, edge trimming, and fine detailing, while keeping the lawn neat and beautiful.

The TerraMow V1000 performs excellently in this regard, enough for me to recommend it, especially for those who want a robotic mower but don't want to dig trenches to bury wires, set up an RTK antenna, or walk the entire yard perimeter holding a phone.

The TerraMow V1000 is currently available on Amazon and the official website, priced at $999 with a $200 coupon. You can also purchase it through the TerraMow official website.
